lectures.title: Binary Tree PostOrder Traversal using Linked List (Recursive Approach)

cues.en: Now, as I've mentioned before, the recursive approach is easier to implement.
As you can see here, in case of in-order traversal, we have three lines of code.
So this is going to happen in case of postorder traversal as well.
So we're just going to put over here Postorder and I will set the rank.
Then here again as a parameter it's going to take node.
And I'm going to set it by default to the root.
So it's going to start from the root.
If it is not selected then here inside this function we are going to check that if node is not equal
to null in this case the logic will be implemented inside this if condition.
So as you mentioned the first thing that we are doing we are visiting the left subtree.
That's why we are just going to go ahead and put over here postorder recursively.
Then we are going to put node dot left.
So first we have to visit the left child.
Then after visiting this we have to visit the right child.
So that's why I will call this postorder recursive method for right child.
Then we are going to go ahead and print out the value to the console, which is going to be the root
node in this case.
So I'm just going to put it like this node dot value.
So this is how the recursive method for postorder traversal works.
So as you can see it is very easy to implement, but we have said that when the tree is very complex,
it is recommended to use the iterative approach.
But when the tree is small, you can use the recursive approach and it's very easy to implement.
So that's how the method looks like.
Now here again the time complexity is going to be o n because here also the method visits every node
in the binary tree exactly once.
So the operation performed each node is a constant time operation for each node.
The method takes two recursive calls, one for the left child, one for the right child.
However, not all nodes have two children.
In a binary tree, the number of the total children across all nodes is always less than the number
of the nodes.
Since each node is visited once and the operations performed per node are constant time, the total
number of the operations for a tree with n nodes is proportional to n.
That's why the time complexity is o n.
Now, the space complexity of recursive algorithm is typically proportional to the maximum depth of
the call stack, and in the worst case scenario, the tree depth can be n, where n is the number of
the nodes.
But in balanced binary tree the space complexity is O log n, but we are taking the worst case.
That's why the space complexity is o n.
So hopefully everything is clear about postorder traversal using recursive approach.
